Key Nvidia partners and suppliers in Asia saw their shares skyrocket on Tuesday as investors piled back into the tech market, following the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by its board.

In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix jumped 6% and 8% respectively.The two companies, which together make up over 40% of the Kospi's weighting, sent the index up almost 6%, leading gains in Asia. The rise in the index triggered the Korea Exchange's sidecar on the index, reportedly making it the 100th sidecar the KRX has activated.

South Korea's LG Electronics soared 12.86%.

Japan's Softbank Group Corp, a major investor in the chip space, climbed over 3%. Semiconductor test company Advantest, as well as counterpart Tokyo Electron, jumped 12% each. Both companies are collaborators with Nvidia.

Nvidia's stock had closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. It had previously shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. This is breaking news, please check back for updates.

U.S. stock futures were slightly higher Monday evening after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO sent the chipmaker's shares soaring and sparked a rebound in the artificial intelligence trade.

Futures tied to the Nasdaq-100 futures were marginally higher. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 91 points, or 0.2%, while S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.

In Asia, South Korea's Kospi jumped over 5% on Tuesday, leading gains in the region. Heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix saw gains of about 7% and 8% respectively.

Japan's Nikkei 225 also rose 2.82%, while the broad based Topix was up 1.6%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was also up 1.3%.

Nvidia surged 31% during Monday's regular session, leading a rally in chip stocks. The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher, the S&P 500 finished up 4.7% and the Dow Industrials rose 3% Monday.

It was the best session for the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 since April 9, 2025 when President Donald Trump announced a reprieve on tariffs.

The tech sector of the S&P 500 soared 9%, powered by sharp gains in semiconductors, memory names and neoclouds. Advanced Micro Devices added almost 7%, while Micron Technology surged 19%. Neocloud stock CoreWeave jumped 22%.

The market action was a sharp reversal from Friday's steep sell-off, which saw the S&P 500 and Dow close in correction as the AI trade suffered and Nvidia tanked.

"The shocking decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO helps to remove a key level of uncertainty from the AI trade, which has been suffering in recent weeks," said Glen Smith, chief investment officer at GDS Wealth Management."Stock market corrections can sometimes end as quickly as they begin and we believe the bottom in stocks is likely in," he added.

Looking ahead to Tuesday's session, on the economic front, consumer confidence data is set to be released.

The stunning decision by Nvidia's board to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO was sealed by a personal promise from President Donald Trump on Sunday that Huang had not broken national security laws, three people familiar with the board's thinking told CNBC.

Several other factors also set the stage for Huang's return and accelerated discussions with him over the weekend, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations close to Nvidia's board.

A sharp stock price drop after his resignation and questions about the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress also spurred the board's decision, the people said.

"I convinced them," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday morning, shortly after Nvidia announced Huang's return.

"I made the deal," the president said. "It was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago.

Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security.

"And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine."

Senior Trump administration officials reached out to the board overnight Friday to inform them that Huang had not violated U.S. national security laws, people familiar with the board's actions said.

After the White House outreach, the board contacted Huang, who joined meetings on Saturday and Sunday to discuss his potential return, the people said.

Huang's spokesman did not respond to a request for comment when asked about his contact with the board and other events leading up to his return.

The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.

The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.

Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.

China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.

On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".

Nvidia shares gapped higher at the open by more than 30%, on pace for its biggest one-day gain in 23 years on Monday, following the news just before the bell that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is going to be reinstated.

Investors and traders said that while this reflex rally may have more to run, cautiousness is warranted on Nvidia and the AI trade because of the overhang of investigations into the alleged Chinese espionage involving the company and others, as well as the possibility for data center moratoriums as Democrats take control of Congress and key governor posts in January.

"Am I as bullish on Nvidia now as I was on Friday? Of course not, you can't be," said Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, which counted Nvidia as its largest position as he bought on the dip over the last few weeks. "I'm trimming back."

It's intraday high on Monday was $171.50, up from its recent low around $125 as it was selling off in the wake controversies. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed at $506.96 the day before his resignation. It reached a high of $469.35 before losing steam as trading wore on Monday.

Jensen Huang was not the only problem at Nvidia, he said, and there are still many vulnerabilities in the overall AI trade, which should give investors pause. Credit-sensitive companies are still at risk of faltering, Khouw added.

For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange.

Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know.

Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.

Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out.

Microsoft has not announced the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online:

None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud.

For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year.

The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client.

Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies.

With Stalwart 1.2.0 the users do not need to change anything. The administrator moves the mailboxes and points the DNS records at Stalwart, and users connect with the same Outlook they used before.

Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024

A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.

Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure

Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.

Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.

The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".

And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.

Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.

Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

The two prime ministers exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service

Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.

The contrast between the two leaders was striking.

Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.

Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.

Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.

For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.

The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.

India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.

According to Nepal's estimates, the cost of rebuilding the region hit by a devastating flash flood in September could amount to $4.8bn

Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked tech and artificial intelligence industries.

The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer at China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.

Shares of Nvidia surged 29% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."

President Donald Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" that Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday hosted his third cryptocurrency gala for top holders of his meme coin, $TRUMP, which has plummeted to below $1 a coin after reaching a high of $75 the day before Trump's second inauguration, on Jan. 19, 2025.

The dinner, held at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, comes as some Democrats say they will investigate potential conflicts of interest and accuse Trump of using the presidency to boost his personal wealth.

At Sunday's dinner, Trump maintained that his support for cryptocurrencies was to boost American economic competitiveness.

"I'm doing it for the United States ... If we don't do it, China's going to do it," he told attendees, The Guardian reported. The event also featured speeches from boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary and NBA champion Tristan Thompson.

A total of 185 "wallets" met the criteria for entry to the gala, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets. The wallets listed on the leaderboard held $8.6 million in $TRUMP tokens, a sharp decline from the May 2025 gala, which featured 220 attendees holding a combined $148 million. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun's wallet alone held $18.5 million at the 2025 event — more than the combined holdings of this year's attendees.

Eligibility was based on time-weighted holdings of Trump's meme coins from Sept. 30 to Nov. 16, according to the organizer's website. The top 29 holders were invited to a VIP reception with the president, with the top four receiving an 18-karat, Trump-branded gold watch.

More than half of the wallets that qualified for the event were linked to crypto exchanges that bar U.S.-based users, according to data gathered by consumer advocacy group Public Citizen for Reuters, suggesting they belong to foreign nationals.

The $TRUMP token has earned the Trump family at least $635 million, according to the president's June financial disclosure. Including the meme coins, the Trump family has earned $2.3 billion from its four main crypto-related businesses since the president's second term began, through to April of this year, according to a Reuters report.

This is despite the ventures' falling value, which, according to the report, they invest little to no money in. Trump's stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430 million as of Friday's close.

Bitcoin climbed back to over $61,000 on Monday in line with the U.S. stock futures bounce, after an AI-related stock sell-off spilled over into other riskier assets last week.
